Teenager Sexting [5251]

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
Sexting and Teens.

Carte Blanche has broadcast a programme on sexting before. But the playing fields have changed, and younger and younger children are sexting, sending nude pictures and provocative texts. Most are ill equipped to deal emotionally with the repercussions on Social Media.

Charmaine Swart’s son was 13 years old and attended a boarding school in Nelspruit. One of his fellow boarders took a video of him in the nude, which showed his face and it went viral amongst the children.

“Daniel” was incredibly traumatised, he was teased, abused and ridiculed by the kids who had seen it. He was traumatised and because he could do nothing about it he became exceptionally depressed. To save her son, his mother took him out of the school. The school did not want to address the problem and in desperation Charmaine went to lay a charge of the creation and dissemination of child pornography against the child who videoed her son.

The father of the child who videoed him is a prominent figure in the Nelspruit community and the file mysteriously dissapeared.

Charmaine’s son now goes to school in Cape Town.

This is not an isolated incident.
One in seven teens report that they are sending sexts, and one in four are receiving sexts, according to our study of over 110 000 teens from around the world.
With the ubiquity of smartphones and increasing digital usage across all age categories, parents should not be surprised that teens are engaging in sexting with other teens. Some as young as 10 years old.
Emma Sadlier (media lawyer) knows of a case of a 10 year old girl who was asked for a nude by a 13 year old boy. She sent him a photo of the colour nude. He then asked her for a picture of her pussy and she sent a picture of her cat.
Although girls and boys sext a similar amount, there are important differences in the perception of this behaviour among youth.
Compared to boys, girls report feeling more pressure to sext, and also worry they will be judged harshly for sexting (e.g., slut shaming) or for not sexting (e.g., being called a “prude”).
Boys, on the other hand, may see sexting as an opportunity to showcase their social status.
This double standard may create higher levels of distress for girls.
The moment the youth presses “send,” they are trusting that the receiver will not share the images or videos without their consent. Sexting can become a problem when this trust is violated.
Rianette Liebowitz who runs an ngo to help and educate children about the perils of social media explains that you should never send anything over a phone that you would not be willing to see it on a huge billboard outside your home.
In many countries, it is illegal for a person to distribute an intimate photo without the explicit consent of the individual in the photo. Nonetheless, our research suggests that 12.5 percent of teens are forwarding intimate photos without the consent of the sender. This in South Africa is also a criminal offence and the complication is that children are now creating and disseminating child pornography.
Coercion and ‘sextortion’
Taken together, several challenges can potentially arise. First, many teens may feel as though sexting is an expectation. Although likely not a warranted expectation, the idea that “my friends are doing it, then maybe I should do it” could be a strong peer motivator.
Shaheda Omar from the Teddy Bear Clinic says that she has seen more and more children fall victim of sexting and the parents are always shocked that their children have been embarking on this risky behaviour.
Parents can keep their teens aware and informed by having open discussions — about healthy dating relationships, peer pressure, digital security, sexuality and citizenship more broadly.
The general consensus is that parents and caregivers should be proactive, rather than protective and reactive, about talking to their teens about sexting. Preaching abstinence is not effective. As with the issue of safe sex, this should be an ongoing conversation with your child instead of a one off “talk.”

(People have right to privacy.)
Adults to understand this but even tougher to for kids.
Internet Permanent Place.
Children don’t have frontal lobe to appreciate long term consequences.

Porn has huge influence on normalisation of this type of behaviour
Male belief that no matter how many times she says no he still thinks she is up for it.

Press Release:


Children Sexting
Sending nude pictures and provocative texts used to be the domain of adults. Now studies show that with the increased access to instant messaging platforms, children as young as ten years old are exchanging explicit content – with each other. The creation and possession of child pornography is a crime and some of these children could also be classified as sexual predators. Carte Blanche explores this growing trend.


Script:


Sexting Script

V/O
Sexting or sending sexually explicit messages and videos used to be considered only the domain of adults.

Link
You wouldn’t give your child a loaded gun, yet many parents are happy to allow their children access to a smart phone and data.

V/O
This is a real Whatsapp conversation that took place between an 11 year old girl and an 13 year old boy.

Emma
“One of the most frequent kinds of sexting, we see is girls and boys who know each other, maybe they’re just starting out a relationship, maybe they have hooked up at a party, may be they’re vibing and then the boy starts asking the girl to send naked pictures. It’s almost like the new second base. ”

V/O
Emma Sadleir is a social media lawyer and has spoken to thousands of children about the impact and consequences of the inappropriate use of social media.

Emma
“These nudes, these naked pictures this internet material has become a social currency amongst the youth and the harder it is to obtain the more valuable it is in the market. It’s a competition who can get the nudes as quick as possible and then you circulate it amongst your friends.”

V/O
Over 55 billion Whatsapp messages are sent across the globe daily, including one billion videos that are uploaded.

But just one message can destroy someone’s life forever. Daniel was just 13 when a sexually explicit video of him was filmed without his consent, and it tore his family apart.

Lucille
“And he cried and said please, please don’t leave me here. I can’t be here.”

V/O
Lucille is a single mother, because she lives in a rural town, her son Daniel has to go to boarding school. After a weekend at home he was reluctant to return. She asked him why?

“And he said it’s about a video. I said, “What video?” And he said, “A video someone made of me”.

“He said that they were just lying around chatting and the way he was sitting, one child asked him, I dare you to try and put your penis in your mouth. I wonder of you could reach it.”

“He said I actually thought I wonder if I can, like boys do. And um he did. He attempted and apparently he reached it and a huge hoo ha and a laugh, so that was it.”

V/O
What Daniel did not know was that one of his friends filmed him doing this.

Lucille
“The next day at school, somebody threw him with an empty cool drink can from the back and said we don’t like gay people in our school and they started teasing him and asked him did you like it, was it good and he said that they did not know what he was talking about.”

V/O
The video went viral in the community.

V/O
Dr Shaheda Omar is the Clinical Director of the Teddybear Clinic and says that children are becoming aware of sex at a lot younger age due to exposure to pornography.


Devi
‘I think when you are a preteen and a teen, it’s already a very difficult time, it’s a confusing time. But what happens when we now add a cell phone, a smart phone to the mix?”

“When children are awakened to programmes that they are not ready yet for, age inappropriate content, and material, they start experimenting and going into areas where they actually are not in a position to process or comprehend the implications thereof. So hyper sexualisation is going beyond your normal developmental curiosity.”

V/O
Teenagers Becky and Isaac began sexting at an early age.

Becky
“I started receiving sexts messages when I was in Grade 7, I was 13 , it felt risky, and anything risky when you are younger feels exciting.

“It was often from older guys, it’s the power of persuasion the way that they communicate with you and say “Oh you are so pretty, you’re really smart, “Oh, can I have this picture?”

Isaac
“My friends think it is a cool thing to see who can get the most nudes on a phone.”

Emma
“A very important point and I get a lot of backlash from parents particularly when I say that the new sexual predator that we should be warning our teenage girls about is not the dodgy dude in the red free candy van outside our school gates, it’s actually the 14, 15 or 16 year old boy sitting next to her in class.”

V/O
To demonstrate the pressure that some girls face, in this conversation a 13 year old boy from Johannesburg asked a girl 57 times for a nude picture, when she eventually relented, within 3 minutes of receiving them he had sent it on to his friends.

Link
“Experts say that before you share anything on line even with a trusted friend , think twice, imagine it on a bill board and if you are happy for the world to see it, then press send.”

Emma
“I think we really bring back this conversation that no means no. With everything that has to do with sexual consent and that includes sexting.”

V/O
But Daniel didn’t have that choice. He was filmed without his consent and humiliated publically.

Lucille
“He was very scared that I was going to be upset with him and I said to him you have done nothing wrong. You were victimized. But the child that filmed this and that sent it out into the big open wide world. Something must happen to him, he must be taught a lesson, that this is not right. You don’t get to mess up somebody’s life like that.”

V/O
Dr Antoinette Basson works as a senior researcher at the Youth Research Unit at Unisa. She interviewed 3000 Gauteng Children from 17 schools across all socio economic backgrounds and asked them questions about sexting. She found that up to 70% of children have taken suggestive pictures of themselves on their cell phones and that there is a direct correlation between sexting and exposure to pornography.

Dr Basson
“In our research we actually found that children are exposed to pornography from a young age due to their exposure to the internet and they very often actually see this kind of behavior and they also react by creating a sext. For example taking a picture a certain way and they have seen that in pornography.”

Isaac
“I watched porn at about the age of 12 around there. I do think porn has had a contribution to sexting. I think guys want to see the real life version of porn. When I say from real life, girls and real live situations.

V/O
Creating, sending and storing images of child pornography is in contravention of the film and publications act, no matter what age you are.

V/O
Although it is illegal for anyone under the age of 18 to watch pornography Antoinette’s survey showed that about 57% of children had already been exposed to it.

Devi
“In your mind, did you find the results alarming?”

Antoinette
“We were a bit shocked we didn’t realize that so many children just in the Gauteng area are exposed to pornography. They exposed to severe kinds, or if I call it an intense kind of pornography, it can even be violence or hard core pornographic material.”

Link
“Teenagers don’t always understand the full ramifications of their actions. There have been many cases around the world where children have committed suicide, because nude selfies have gone viral.”

Emma
“What the children are not necessarily appreciating is just how permanent that content can be.”

V/O
Emma likens it to a digital tattoo, it’s with you forever. Many children however don’t know where to turn once they have lost control of the image.

Antoinette
“A lot of children said they don’t report they don’t even talk to somebody. So they are walking around like little time bombs, because they have a lot of mixed emotions. They are bullied at school because as soon as the image get in the hands of other learners they are victimized. “

Emma
“Even if you were being shamed or bullied non-stop while you were at school, in the old days 10 years ago, still leave school at the end of the day and get out of your school uniform for the night or weekend and forget about it. And now because these kids have their devices with them at all times. That shaming follows them and we are seeing a huge spike in suicide as a result.”

V/O
Luckily Daniel’s mother removed him from the school permanently and he was able to have counseling with an independent psychologist.

“And she said to me if you send your son back to that school he will kill himself, she said he is broken. He is a soft hearted child and sensitive and she said I don’t know what you are going to do but you can’t send him back there.”

Shaheda
“Symptoms of victims of rape experience or manifest is very similar if not the same as to that of victims of sexting. Where when they are exposed they often suffer and manifest symptoms of post traumatic stress disorder, self destructive behavioral patterns.

V/O
Lucille moved her son to a boarding school hundreds of kilometer’s away and laid charges at the police station against the boy who filmed her son.

Devi
“According to South African Law if you are under the age of 18 but now you have young children who are distributing and creating child pornography.”

Shaheda
“And that constitutes an offence, because we know that taking pictures, semi nude or nude pictures and sending it to a friend is distribution but when they are creating it, it is also a criminal offence.”

Isaac
“I haven’t thought about the legal implications that are involved sexting and sending nudes, I don’t think it ever occurred to me.”

Devi
‘What advice do you have for parents?”

Shaheda
“Communication, Communication, communication. Because children do not understand the long term implications of their immediate gratification. Because they think of in the here and now.

Becky
“You don’t realize the seriousness of the situation until it gets really bad and by then it’s too late.”

Emma
“So these are very, very serious laws and I’m afraid we are seeing children getting prosecuted for being involved in consensual sexting.”

V/O
Lucille feels that the boy who filmed her son has caused irreparable emotional damage and she is determined to try to take the matter to court.

Lucille
“I need justice for my son. I need my son to see that if you do something wrong you will be punished.”

Link
A Unisa study looking at 12- 18 year olds shows that up to 70% of kids have taken suggestive pictures of themselves. Is your child one of them?

V/O
Billions of Whatsapp messages are sent out daily.
But one just message shattered a young boy’s life when a sexually explicit video of him went viral. His psychologist was deeply concerned.

“And she said to me if you take him back to that school he will commit suicide.”

In the past children used to send love letters in class, now they are sexting or sending sexually explicit messages or nude photographs to each other which sometimes go viral with tragic consequences.

Link
You wouldn’t give your child a loaded gun, yet many parents are happy to allow their children access to a smart phone and data.

V/O
The number of underage kids sexting is on the rise and if caught they could be held criminally liable for creating and distributing child pornography.

metadata.Further information: Sexting and Teens. Carte Blanche has broadcast a programme on sexting before. But the playing fields have changed, and younger and younger children are sexting, sending nude pictures and provocative texts. Most are ill equipped to deal emotionally with the repercussions on Social Media. Charmaine Swart’s son was 13 years old and attended a boarding school in Nelspruit. One of his fellow boarders took a video of him in the nude, which showed his face and it went viral amongst the children. “Daniel” was incredibly traumatised, he was teased, abused and ridiculed by the kids who had seen it. He was traumatised and because he could do nothing about it he became exceptionally depressed. To save her son, his mother took him out of the school. The school did not want to address the problem and in desperation Charmaine went to lay a charge of the creation and dissemination of child pornography against the child who videoed her son. The father of the child who videoed him is a prominent figure in the Nelspruit community and the file mysteriously dissapeared. Charmaine’s son now goes to school in Cape Town. This is not an isolated incident. One in seven teens report that they are sending sexts, and one in four are receiving sexts, according to our study of over 110 000 teens from around the world. With the ubiquity of smartphones and increasing digital usage across all age categories, parents should not be surprised that teens are engaging in sexting with other teens. Some as young as 10 years old. Emma Sadlier (media lawyer) knows of a case of a 10 year old girl who was asked for a nude by a 13 year old boy. She sent him a photo of the colour nude. He then asked her for a picture of her pussy and she sent a picture of her cat. Although girls and boys sext a similar amount, there are important differences in the perception of this behaviour among youth. Compared to boys, girls report feeling more pressure to sext, and also worry they will be judged harshly for sexting (e.g., slut shaming) or for not sexting (e.g., being called a “prude”). Boys, on the other hand, may see sexting as an opportunity to showcase their social status. This double standard may create higher levels of distress for girls. The moment the youth presses “send,” they are trusting that the receiver will not share the images or videos without their consent. Sexting can become a problem when this trust is violated. Rianette Liebowitz who runs an ngo to help and educate children about the perils of social media explains that you should never send anything over a phone that you would not be willing to see it on a huge billboard outside your home. In many countries, it is illegal for a person to distribute an intimate photo without the explicit consent of the individual in the photo. Nonetheless, our research suggests that 12.5 percent of teens are forwarding intimate photos without the consent of the sender. This in South Africa is also a criminal offence and the complication is that children are now creating and disseminating child pornography. Coercion and ‘sextortion’ Taken together, several challenges can potentially arise. First, many teens may feel as though sexting is an expectation. Although likely not a warranted expectation, the idea that “my friends are doing it, then maybe I should do it” could be a strong peer motivator. Shaheda Omar from the Teddy Bear Clinic says that she has seen more and more children fall victim of sexting and the parents are always shocked that their children have been embarking on this risky behaviour. Parents can keep their teens aware and informed by having open discussions — about healthy dating relationships, peer pressure, digital security, sexuality and citizenship more broadly. The general consensus is that parents and caregivers should be proactive, rather than protective and reactive, about talking to their teens about sexting. Preaching abstinence is not effective. As with the issue of safe sex, this should be an ongoing conversation with your child instead of a one off “talk.” Other themes to explore Freedom of expression not unlimited right.
